topic: Research: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026: Developer Security Checklist

key_points: Official OWASP GenAI Security Project release dated December 9, 2025.
Frames the 2026 Top 10 as a peer-reviewed framework for autonomous and agentic AI systems that plan, act, and make decisions across complex workflows.
Positions the list as practical guidance for builders, defenders, and decision-makers, with related 2026 resources on governance, AI red teaming, and crosswalks.
Turns the OWASP Agentic Top 10 into a red-team testing framework with per-risk testing strategies.

Lists the ten risks as ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, and ASI10 Rogue Agents.
Explains how agentic risk differs from traditional LLM app risk because agents have autonomous decision-making, persistent memory, tool/API access, and multi-agent coordination.
Maps several ASI risks back to the OWASP LLM Top 10, which is useful for explaining why developers should test both frameworks.
Focuses on identity as the practical control layer for agentic applications.
Introduces the developer-friendly framing of moving from least privilege to least agency: restrict not only what an agent can access, but how freely it can act.
Recommends agent-specific identities, task-bound tokens, short-lived credentials, rapid revocation, and human-in-the-loop gates for sensitive scopes.
Strong angle for developer checklist sections on OAuth scopes, token lifetime, identity boundaries, and approval flows.
Summarizes the OWASP release for developers and security practitioners, emphasizing the shift from passive LLM outputs to active agent behavior.
Treats agents as principals with goals, tools, memory, and inter-agent protocols, each of which becomes a distinct attack surface.
Provides concrete examples such as indirect prompt injection through external content and memory/context poisoning.
Useful competitor because it explains the taxonomy simply but does not go as deep into implementable engineering controls.
Emphasizes operational security capabilities aligned to OWASP: comprehensive visibility, agent-centric inventory, supply-chain integrity, governance, guardrails, and active runtime control.
Recommends inventories enriched with behavior, permissions, memory use, and data access to find misconfigurations, overprivileged agents, and risky workflows.
Highlights continuous verification of prompts, plugins, RAG datasets, orchestration scripts, and model dependencies.
Good source for making the article more actionable around runtime monitoring and AI asset inventory.

stats.fact: OWASP says the Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 was developed with more than 100 industry experts, researchers, and practitioners.
McKinsey's 2026 AI trust research reports that nearly two-thirds of respondents cite security and risk concerns as the top barrier to fully scaling agentic AI.
McKinsey also reports that 74% of respondents identify inaccuracy and 72% cite cybersecurity as highly relevant AI risks as adoption expands.
Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise survey of 3,235 IT and business leaders found only 21% have a mature governance model for agentic AI.
Deloitte reports that by 2027, 74% of surveyed organizations expect to use AI agents at least moderately; 23% expect extensive use and 5% expect full core-business integration.
IBM's June 2026 study says surveyed organizations experienced an average of 54 AI agent incidents last year, and 17% were high severity.
IBM reports that among high-severity AI agent incidents, 37% resulted in data exposure or security breaches, 33% caused cascading system failures, and 17% triggered compliance issues.
IBM reports that organizations embedding controls directly into AI systems experience 25% fewer incidents, while manual governance increases incident risk as adoption scales.
Ivanti's 2026 research says 87% of security teams consider adopting agentic AI a priority, and 77% report at least some comfort allowing AI to act without human review.

Cloud Security Alliance's 2026 non-human identity research notes that 78% of organizations have no documented policy for creating or removing AI identities, and only 8% express high confidence that legacy IAM can manage AI and NHI risks.
Grant Thornton's 2026 AI Impact Survey says 78% of business executives lack strong confidence they could pass an independent AI governance audit within 90 days.

angles: Make the article a developer security checklist, not just another taxonomy summary: for each ASI risk, give the exact engineering controls to add before production.
Lead with the shift from least privilege to least agency: autonomy, tool access, memory persistence, and inter-agent delegation all need separate limits.
Treat every agent as a non-human identity with its own owner, scopes, tokens, audit trail, revocation path, and lifecycle policy.
Separate build-time controls from runtime controls: threat modeling and dependency review are not enough once an agent can call tools, modify state, or learn from memory.
Use the IBM incident data to justify why cascading failures, data exposure, and compliance issues belong in ordinary developer checklists, not only enterprise governance decks.
Map OWASP ASI risks to code-review prompts: tool schema validation, parameter allowlists, approval gates, sandboxing, memory write controls, and trace logging.
Explain that guardrails are a layer, not the control plane: policy enforcement, identity scoping, runtime monitoring, and kill switches must exist outside the model prompt.
Include a practical maturity path: prototype agent, internal tool, production agent, multi-agent workflow, and autonomous agent each need progressively stricter controls.
Use current real-world risk patterns: indirect prompt injection, MCP/tool supply chain compromise, memory poisoning, over-scoped API keys, and shadow agents.
Differentiate OWASP LLM Top 10 from OWASP Agentic Top 10 so readers understand why prompt-injection defenses alone are insufficient.
